item.title: Trump orders federal contractors to notify White House of congressional inquiries
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to inform the administration of congressional inquiries into their work with the executive branch as the White House seeks to limit oversight by Democrats. The order, signed Friday, comes after White House Counsel Will Scharf previously instructed all executive agencies to obtain explicit permission from the White House before allowing employees to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by ABC News on Monday. Eloisa Lopez/Reuters - PHOTO: President Donald Trump attends an arrival ceremony at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Philippines, November 18, 2026. Federal contractors and subcontractors will now be required to immediately notify the White House and their contracting agencies of "any pending or future congressional request respecting the contractors' communications or work with the executive branch," the order states. All contractors must follow orders from the administration with regard to withholding communications it deems protected by executive privilege. Top White House lawyer warns Democrats that threats of oversight could be criminally probed According to the order, contractors who fail to notify the White House of requests from Congress or refuse to follow the administration's instructions face potential contract termination, as well as suspension or debarment, which would prevent a contractor from winning future federal contracts. "The ability of the Congress to seek executive branch information is limited; it cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies (agencies), employees, or Federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions," the order signed by Trump states. The executive order does not name a specific contractor, but covers "all federal contractors," and extends that coverage to "subcontractors working for a federal contractor on a federal contract." Alex Brandon/AP Photo - PHOTO: President Donald Trump talks after visiting the White House Ballroom construction site at the White House, Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. There are roughly 100,000 companies that hold federal contracts, plus the subcontractors, according to Bloomberg Government . The order argues that a "lack of coordination" between the administration and its contractors undermines efficiency and claims that "contractors also may be unaware of the executive branch's interests and positions, resulting in duplicative and wasteful efforts." "It is therefore the policy of the United States to protect confidential information and enhance economy and efficiency in Federal contracting by preventing and prohibiting uncoordinated disclosures of information pursuant to congressional requests," the order states. The White House's Office of Management and Budget will develop guidelines to ensure compliance and "adequate coordination between the contracting agencies, contractors, and White House," the order said. Alex Brandon/AP Photo - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during a tour of the White House Ballroom at the White House, Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. In a fact sheet released on Friday by the White House, the administration argued that it "must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without concern that confidential information may be released to unauthorized third parties, even by federal contractors from a congressional request." "If the Executive Branch cannot be assured that communications with contractors will remain confidential, federal agencies will be deterred from safely and freely sharing sensitive information with them, which will deadlock critical government programs," it added. Democrats take the House. Here’s what they plan to investigate and their legislative agenda The order marks yet another attempt to push back on potential oversight of the White House, as Congressional Democrats have warned that they are preparing to launch new investigations. Incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia warned the administration to "lawyer up" in the wake of November's elections. Finn Gomez/Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House, November 20, 2026 in Washington. In a letter sent to the California Democratic lawmaker last week, Scharf warned that Democrats could be criminally probed over their threats of exercising Congress's oversight powers, claiming that "abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas ... make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end." Garcia responded to the letter last week, saying in a statement that "Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate." "We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers," he added. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-orders-federal-contractors-coordinate-white-house-congressional/story?id=138344717

item.title: Water supply hack warning: FBI says threats are rising
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Recent cyber outages have disrupted airlines, retailers and hospitals, but experts warn the next major target could be something far more essential: the water coming from your tap. Federal agencies, researchers and cybersecurity experts are sounding alarms about rising threats to U.S. water systems as hackers increasingly target vulnerable infrastructure connected to the Internet. Why are officials worried now? The FBI warned in July that malicious cyber actors have been targeting Internet-facing programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, used by water and wastewater systems. According to the FBI, these intrusions have already caused operational disruptions, highlighting how vulnerable critical infrastructure can be when equipment is exposed online. Government advisor says Doomsday supply stockers aren’t overreacting How serious is the threat? The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency warned in September that cyberattacks against public water systems are increasing. The agency says utilities face threats ranging from ransomware to sophisticated intrusions that could disrupt operations or affect service reliability. What are local governments facing? A recent report from The Pew Charitable Trusts found that many drinking water and wastewater systems operate with aging technology, limited budgets and staffing shortages that can hinder cybersecurity efforts. Pew reported that local governments are increasingly investing in cyber defenses, but many smaller systems still struggle to keep pace with evolving threats. How is AI changing the risk landscape? Researchers Susan Athey, Neil Gandal, and Tyler Moore at Stanford Graduate School of Business say in their report "A Wake-Up Call on Cyber Risk as AI Ups the Stakes" that artificial intelligence is accelerating the cyber threat environment by helping attackers identify vulnerabilities more quickly and execute attacks at greater scale. "The most severe cyber incidents can lead to losses amounting to billions of dollars and also have the potential to result in physical harm, loss of life, or even political turmoil," they state in the report. Rubio on tech failures: US ‘not under systemic attack’ Why are experts calling this a wake-up call? According to a recent Time analysis , cyberattacks have already affected water facilities in several states, including an incident in Minnesota that disrupted equipment at a treatment plant and threatened the local water supply. Many small water systems remain vulnerable because they lack dedicated cybersecurity resources, making resilience and emergency preparedness increasingly important as threats grow. Bolton sounds alarm after Microsoft, FAA outages What can utilities do? Federal guidance urges utilities to strengthen cyber hygiene by disconnecting unnecessary Internet-facing devices, implementing multifactor authentication, conducting regular vulnerability assessments and maintaining incident response plans. The FBI and EPA have encouraged operators to monitor industrial control systems closely and promptly apply security updates when available. What can people do at home? Experts say households should prepare for potential service disruptions much like they would for severe weather or power outages. That can include maintaining an emergency supply of bottled water, storing water safely for sanitation needs, keeping basic emergency kits and monitoring instructions from local authorities if a utility reports an incident. NewsNation's Jesse Weber recently spoke with preparedness expert Jim Cobb, who said, "My longstanding recommendation has always been have enough cash immediately accessible" for fuel, lodging and meals during an emergency. Cobb also advised households to review supplies already on hand before rushing to stores, adding that food, water and basic necessities should be a priority. Microsoft outage raises concerns over US cybersecurity Why does this matter beyond cybersecurity? Water systems are among the most critical pieces of infrastructure in the country, serving millions of Americans every day. While major cyberattacks remain relatively rare, federal officials, researchers and industry experts agree that growing digital threats, combined with increasingly connected systems, mean cybersecurity is no longer just an IT problem. It is becoming a public safety issue. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. item.title: Elon Musk's government funding for SpaceX is on the line, a top Democrat warns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A top Democrat warned Elon Musk that “every” U.S. government contract with SpaceX has been called into question, the latest sign that congressional Democrats are preparing to investigate Donald Trump’s administration officials and his allies. Connecticut Rep. Jim Himes, who is poised to lead the House Intelligence Committee in January, issued the warning in a letter to the SpaceX CEO Friday, demanding answers about last month’s disruptions in Ukraine to Starshield , a U.S. government-purchased service that uses SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network. Musk acknowledged in an October post on X that the company intentionally restricted its Starlink service in Ukraine , hindering military efforts to combat Russia. He claimed Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms by using the civilian commercial service for “offensive drone strikes.” Starshield, he added, is controlled by the U.S. government. “I write to formally request that senior SpaceX officials meet with me to explain the Starshield service disruptions in Ukraine in October 2026,” Himes wrote in his letter. “My committee staff have requested this briefing on multiple occasions but have received no substantive response from your company.” Himes said Starshield’s reliance on Starlink satellites — more than 10,000 of which are in orbit — does not give SpaceX the right to make “unilateral” changes to the government-contracted service. A top Democrat warned Elon Musk that ‘every’ U.S. government contract with SpaceX has been called into question following service disruptions in Ukraine last month (Getty Images) “My view, which I have conveyed to senior Administration officials, is that SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” he wrote. “For that reason, it is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for ... SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems until I receive satisfactory answers,” he added. SpaceX, which went public in June , had about $22 billion in government contracts as of last February. “SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR,” Musk wrote on X last month. “That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict.” The war in Ukraine, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, has dragged on for more than four years, claiming hundreds of thousands of lives. Repeated efforts by the Trump administration to broker a peace deal have so far failed. The Independent has contacted the company for comment. More than 10,000 Starlink satellites are currently in orbit. Pictured: SpaceX Starship Flight 14 launches from its launch pad at Boca Chica Beach on September 28 in Boca Chica Beach, Texas (Getty Images) Himes’ letter is the latest sign that Democrats plan to probe Trump administration officials and allies when they take control of Congress in January following their midterm election victories. Asked about Musk last week, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries vowed to investigate “everyone” involved in the “ MAGA extremist movement .” Musk, who spearheaded DOGE and donated millions to Republicans, recently declared he is “ not MAGA” despite campaigning for the president in his signature black MAGA hat. Also last week, Rep. Robert Garcia, the Oversight Committee’s top Democrat, wrote letters to a dozen administration officials and others in Trump’s orbit , requesting that they preserve documents, signaling an investigation could be forthcoming. Among those who received letters were President Donald Trump’s eldest sons, Vice President JD Vance and Attorney General Todd Blanche. In an apparent bid to thwart Democratic investigations, the White House has instructed federal officials and government contractors to obtain permission before testifying on Capitol Hill. Blanche has said the Department of Justice will cooperate with Congress but insisted “ we will not back down ” from Trump’s agenda. This article originally appeared on The Independent at https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/elon-musk-spacex-investigation-democrat-b3089261.html

item.title: Republicans seeking an alternative to JD Vance ask: How about a governor?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As Republicans weigh alternatives to Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028, at least one question has increasingly bubbled up since the midterms: How about a governor? Several current and former GOP governors are either keeping the door open to running or pushing for one of their own to be the nominee. The discussion shows how Republicans see room to maneuver around Vance after their party's devastating midterm losses. At least four current or former GOP governors are signaling their national ambitions: Govs. Ron DeSantis of Florida, Brian Kemp of Georgia and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas, as well as former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. And at least two others – Govs. Spencer Cox of Utah and Kevin Stitt of Oklahoma – have said this year that they prefer the 2028 nominee be a governor, an implicit snub of Vance. "In this climate, where people are ticked off at DC in general — Republican, Democrat alike — being removed from that, being able to get things done and being removed are kind of like the magic one-two punch," said former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, a Republican who ran for president in 2016. Vance and his allies aren't ignoring the talk. They launched an offensive against Stitt on Thursday after he suggested lawmakers from both parties focus on immigration reform in President Donald Trump's final two years. Vance said any effort at "amnesty" would be "morally and electorally disastrous." Stitt thanked Vance "for bringing governors into the conversation." It's all part of the GOP's post-election reassessment of whether there is an opening for a Republican not named Vance. "I don't think there's any doubt it's gotten wider since [Nov. 3]," said Marc Short, who was chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence. "I think it was such a shellacking and a rejection of the last two years that they'll have to be candidates who look and say, 'Maybe there's an opening for me.' But I still think it's a pretty narrow path." Walker also offered a note of caution for governors, saying they cannot run alone on their statehouse records. "You've got to translate that to, 'Look what I did, and here's what I'm going to do next,'" Walker said. Even after the midterms, some potential 2028 candidates have acknowledged Vance would be hard to beat, especially with Trump's support. Huckabee Sanders said Friday on HBO's "Real Time with Bill Maher" that Vance is "still the most dominant figure on the Republican side … and starts with a tremendous lead." DeSantis appeared more bearish on Vance in a New York Times interview published Friday. "VPs tend to be derivative," DeSantis said. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who is leaving office after Trump helped defeat him in his primary, questioned in a recent interview whether Vance would remain in Trump's "good favor" ahead of 2028, noting his recent comments blaming the Iran war for the GOP's midterm losses. "I think that's a big issue," Cornyn said. "But in 2028, I think what we'll see is, if I had to guess, I would say an outsider has a better chance than someone who's a member of the current administration, but that's two years from now." The governors' cases DeSantis and Huckabee Sanders have boasted that their states withstood the "blue wave" the swept across the country. DeSantis said the day after the election that it was "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans" in other parts of the country. "We built up a lot of trust with our voters over the years," DeSantis told CNN's Jake Tapper the same day, adding that a property tax ballot measure that he championed helped motivate an otherwise sleepy GOP base. "We were able to turn out enough voters to be able to get these guys across the finish line." During a post-election speech to the Young America's Foundation in California, Youngkin said many voters "aren't seeing and feeling this economy that statistically is strong." "They voted for change, and a lot of them voted for it," Youngkin said. "And so our job is not to sulk. Our job is not to make excuses. Our job is to prove with better ideas and real results that common-sense conservative policies are the surest path to the affordable, prosperous life that Americans are asking for." Walker, who serves as president of the foundation, said Youngkin's speech was "extremely well-received." Huckabee Sanders, who's been on a media tour promoting a new book, has said Republicans need to be more outspoken about their accomplishments and differences with Democrats. "I don't think that our message needs to be different or needs to change," she said during a stop Tuesday at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank in Washington, DC. "I think we just have to do a better job telling it. We have not done a great job of telling our story and talking about the things that really impact people's lives." "That has to be a core focus moving forward as we go into the next election cycle," she added. DeSantis, Huckabee Sanders and Youngkin have all faced questions in recent days about their interest in 2028 and not ruled it out. The vulnerabilities governors would face Most of the governors would have certain obvious vulnerabilities to overcome in the 2028 primary. DeSantis and Kemp would have to overcome their past tensions with Trump. DeSantis challenged Trump in the 2024 primary, and Kemp clashed with Trump over his 2020 reelection loss in Georgia. Both have appeared to reconcile more recently with Trump, who has made public appearances with them and complimented them. A person familiar with Kemp's thinking said he was considering running for president but had not closed the door on other opportunities. Senate Republicans are expected to court him to challenge Georgia Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2028. One Georgia Republican strategist said Kemp would be "much different" from anti-Trump Republicans who waged longshot bids for president. "I think the way [Kemp] dealt with Trump — he wasn't opposed to Trump, he was just doing what was best for the state," the strategist said. "Trump was mad at him at certain times, but he wasn't mad at Trump." Youngkin and Kemp would also have to grapple with failing to keep their seats Republican after they left office. Youngkin has been clashing with his Democratic successor, Abigail Spanberger, in recent days over her decision to rescind his plan to participate in a federal school voucher program. Kemp had an especially rough midterm cycle, endorsing candidates for Senate and governor who lost their primaries. He campaigned for the eventual nominees — Mike Collins for Senate and Rick Jackson for governor — but both lost to Democrats. The highest-profile incoming GOP governor may be Byron Donalds in Florida. Trump endorsed him early in his campaign, and Vance campaigned with him in the final weeks of the election. Donalds said last year that Vance was the "leader in the clubhouse" for the 2028 nomination and suggested in March that he would support Vance over fellow Floridian Marco Rubio for president. Donalds struck a different tone in a post-midterms interview. "We'll see what happens down the line with the nomination from my party," Donalds said on NBC's "Meet the Press." "The only thing I know is there's going to need to be a robust conversation, a robust debate." item.title: California train burglars executed 'staggering' heists for $22 million haul, DOJ says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Cajon Pass at Cajon, California, circa 1964. Photograph: Universal History Archive/UIG/Getty Images Fourteen people in southern California have been accused of burglarizing more than $22m worth of goods from moving freight trains, in a plot reminiscent of the US old west, when outlaws and bandits wreaked havoc on the nascent railroad industry. The justice department has brought railroad theft charges against the group for raiding at least 36 trains and selling thousands of stolen Nike sneakers, among other products, on the black market. “The scale of the theft is staggering,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said. Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, was the alleged ringleader for the so-called “Los Trenes” (“the trains”) scheme, which spanned 2024 through 2026. Court documents did not list an attorney for Angel or the other charged individuals. Each robbery took a similar form. Angel’s associates, including his father and two uncles, stowed away on moving freight trains, according to a grand jury indictment. With some of the men on board serving as lookouts, the others would slash the train’s air hose, causing a sudden loss of air pressure and forcing an emergency stop of the entire vehicle. The maneuver is perilous given the risks of derailment. Once the train was disabled, the rest of the Los Trenes crew would swoop in to load up the stolen goods and stash the loot at houses across southern California, prosecutors say. Angel posed for a selfie, where he threw up the peace sign, in front of several boxes containing Nike merchandise, in a February 2024 photograph, attached to court documents. The next burglary would come months later. In October 2024, Donta Hedgeman, 27, sawed through the lock of a container on a moving Nike train, according to video evidence. The heists ramped up in 2025, even as signs emerged that law enforcement was catching on to the alleged thefts. An unidentified “co-conspirator” texted 23-year-old Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez on 17 April 2025 to say he had been arrested for receiving stolen property. “They want me to tell them who did I get them from and who had the other pairs,” the person wrote. Martinez responded, instructing the person to contact him over Signal, an app with encrypted messaging. Twelve days later, the crew made off with 1,170 tools and 17,000 parts from Milwaukee Tool. Police officers appeared to sniff around an unnamed company, which purchased a slew of stolen products from the crew in the fall of 2025. A different “co-conspirator” speculated on their fate. “Good luck with them wires/if they go deep in the case/You’re cooked,” they wrote to Martinez. Then, on 16 January 2026, Angel and 25-year-old Fredy Marquina referenced a partner being intercepted by police: “They just got Jorge for buying and receiving/stolen property.” Once again, faced with the mounting risk of being caught, the men proceeded with further heists in the summer of 2026. In July 2026, Angel Sanchez, 24, shared an AI-generated image that appeared to glamorize their robbery spree. Masked men tossed Nike sneakers off a Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSR) train into luxury cars inscribed with the words “Los Trenes”. In the image, a helicopter circled above, shining a searchlight. If convicted of the conspiracy charge, the men face at least five years in prison. The theft of interstate railroad charge has a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. A conviction for violence against railroad carriers would carry the most severe punishment with a possibility of life in prison. Prosecutors described this week’s sweeping indictment as the culmination of a 14-month-long investigation. “We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market,” said Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles county district attorney. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1. The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days. Over the past week, the Army briefed at least three Gold Star families on the investigation, and several family members told CBS News they were frustrated by what they heard. Some of those briefed told CBS News the report does little to address the findings of an eight-month CBS News investigation, in which multiple sources said Army commanders ignored repeated warnings about the drone threat in the weeks before the attack. Witnesses told CBS News that the facilities were not fortified to protect service members from a strike by one-way attack drones, which are a staple of the Iranian arsenal. Soldiers on the site said they had seen U.S. intelligence prior to the war showing the location was on an Iranian target list. And they argued the facilities lacked sufficient medical supplies and a plan for a mass casualty incident. The briefings were led by Brig. Gen. Peter Glass, the deputy commander of U.S. Army Central, according to those who attended. They were individually held at either military or National Guard posts in locations close to the respective families. "I wish I felt better," a Gold Star family member told CBS News after her briefing, which she said lasted roughly three hours. "I wish this gave me more than what I had yesterday or what I had the day before." The briefings come just days after a U.S. Army soldier who survived the deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran. The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Nov. 13 and obtained by CBS News. In the complaint, Ramsbottom alleges that Army leaders were warned about drone threats at the U.S. command post, and alleges the site had "no dedicated protection" against the Iranian drones. In an interview with CBS News, he identified Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, who commanded the unit, and Maj. Gen. John Hinson, who oversaw logistics for the U.S. command, as dismissing warnings about protection at the location. Ramsbottom called for an independent investigation. Neither official responded to multiple requests for comment from CBS News. Another Gold Star family member described the briefing as mostly "cordial" but said the exchange grew tense when family members pressed for more answers about why the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba when most other soldiers were sent out of Kuwait ahead of the launch of Operation Epic Fury. "We took a couple breaks because it got heavy and I needed some air," one family member said. Joey Amor, whose wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was among those killed, told 60 Minutes he believes she might have survived if there was a better plan in place. "I think my wife had a shot, yeah," he said. He said investigators told him that, no matter what medical resources were present, his wife's injuries were too severe for her to have survived the strike. The Pentagon for months has declined comment to CBS News, but confirmed its internal investigation into the Port Shuaiba attack concluded in June. Still, it would take until mid-November for the Army to share its findings — another point of contention for some Gold Star family members. "Going in I had an idea of what I wanted to know," another family member said. "I just knew I wasn't going to get answers — and I was right." item.title: At least 11 people killed in Mexico's Sinaloa after capture of cartel boss, officials say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in an operation that left at least 11 people dead. Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized. Mexico’s Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city. Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. “The fighting was happening all over Guasave,” said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. “It spread throughout the city.” Mexican authorities said that they used “stealth and surprise” to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to discuss the case. “Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary,” the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least “10 roadblocks” with burning vehicles on Guasave’s streets. Terror in Sinaloa Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations. “Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks,” Sánchez told The Associated Press. She said that the city’s firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning. An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation. Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday. “The aftermath of last night’s war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down,” Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico. Guasave residents remained “very afraid” because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said. Capture prompts celebration and warnings Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office. The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities. “Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. “We will continue the hunt.” Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention “an important step in pacifying Sinaloa.” Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins , including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes , known as “ El Mencho ,” who was killed by the military in February. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run. The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa. “What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States,” Saucedo said. “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.” ___ Janetsky and Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Associated Press writer Thomas Strong contributed to this report from Washington. item.title: Christian nationalists see GOP's midterm losses as opportunity to supplant Trump's MAGA
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
IRVING, Texas (AP) — Christian nationalists once celebrated President Donald Trump’s return to the White House as a victory for their movement. Now they see the Republican Party's recent election losses as an opportunity to supplant his “Make America Great Again” movement with their extremist vision. Many gathered in Texas last week for a three-day conference where Nick Fuentes , an avowed white nationalist, was the surprise special guest. The way he sees it, the midterms effectively dethroned Trump as the party's leader. “This is like the death of Josef Stalin,” Fuentes said, his high-register voice reverberating in a dark and cavernous convention hall. “And there is nothing that will fill the void right now.” But that’s exactly what Joel Webbon wants to do. A 40-year-old pastor and podcaster with a precisely sculpted salt and pepper beard, Webbon organized the conference, “Christ is King: America After Trump,” and served as its master of ceremonies. Goal of increasing the clout of Christian nationalism Webbon's movement, which seeks a theocratic government and patriarchal society, remains on the political fringe, and there were no elected officials on stage. Webbon said conservative leaders won’t give him the time of day “because they want their base to not even know I exist.” As rival factions wrestle over the Republicans’ future, Webbon is planning to expand the influence of Christian nationalism. The conference, where organizers said more than 1,000 people attended, was a start as the movement looks toward Washington. “We can clearly say they have been gaining power,” said Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at University of North Florida who has focused on Christian nationalism. “I wouldn’t dismiss them.” In Webbon’s vision, the United States is largely made up of white Christians, the Apostles’ Creed is the preamble to the U.S. Constitution, at least 50 million people are deported, interracial marriage is considered “not normal,” and Jews, Muslims, Hindus and women don’t have the right to vote or hold public office. While Webbon doesn't expect that to come to fruition anytime soon, he and his allies hope the Election Day shattering of Trump's coalition will allow them to pick up the pieces and start down that road. “Phase one is kind of complete,” Webbon said on stage. A girl in the third row kicked her yellow shoes that didn’t reach the floor. Young men, several wearing blue “America First” caps sold by Fuentes, listened attentively. “We’re moving into phase two,” Webbon said. “It’s time to get the numbers. It’s time to get the donors. It’s time to get our guys into positions of power.” Disappointment with Trump was widespread Right-wing Christians have long been some of Trump’s most dedicated supporters. Although Trump never had a reputation as religious, they viewed him as a political battering ram against their cultural opponents, and he positioned himself as a defender of evangelical values. Christian nationalism goes a step further. “This isn’t your next-door neighbor’s Christianity,” Ingersoll said. “They want America to be a Christian nation in a very specific kind of way. And that’s going to be exclusively for Christians, mostly for white Christians.” Trump's choice of Pete Hegseth as defense secretary was viewed as progress for the movement. Hegseth belongs to a church network co-founded by a Christian nationalist pastor, and he reposted a video last year that included arguments that women shouldn't be allowed to vote. Trump dined with Fuentes at the president's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida in between his two White House terms and has repeatedly declined to denounce Fuentes. The White House did not respond to a request for comment for this story. There was little goodwill toward the president at the “Christ is King” conference. One of the more charitable assessments from speakers was that Trump imperiled the Republican project enough to allow an opening. “Did anybody get fooled with Trump?” asked JP Sears, a right-wing YouTube comedian. A few dozen hands lifted into the air. “Boy, he was good, he was, I fell for that,” Sears said. “'He’s going to dismantle the deep state, he is going to root out the corruption in the system.' And here we are, he is the corruption.” After Sears spoke, attendees heard from one of the conference's sponsors, a wealth manager, and then checked out the booths in a hall adjacent to the stage. There was a stand selling T-shirts saying “I’ll take the Christian, hold the Judeo.” People stood on vibrating platforms that proclaimed the benefits of lymphatic drainage and stress reduction. Children’s books focused on the foibles of socialism. Kyle Fischer, a 34-year-old volunteer, was selling Webbon's book, “White Genocide.” Fischer said American Jews should leave for Israel. “Go. You have your nation. This is ours," he said. “Do I want them dead or anything? No. Come to Christ. You're my brother,” he said, adding later, "call me antisemitic, call me a Nazi, I don’t care anymore.” Webbon wants to spread his ideology Some Republicans, notably Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, have warned about growing antisemitism on the political right. Even some attendees seemed uncomfortable with how Webbon and his allies talked about different races not being compatible or equal. Webbon, who has almost 140,000 followers on X, said his worldview prioritizes religion over race, whereas white nationalists do the opposite or eschew religion altogether. The distinction makes little difference to people who study his movement. “So it doesn’t have to just be white folk,” said Michael Emerson, a Rice University professor of sociology who has focused on ideologies around religion and race. “But you’ve got to support ultimately that white folks are in the dominant.” Webbon doesn't expect attendees to agree with him on everything, and he's looking for any chance to pull people into his ideological orbit. Seth Goforth, a 19-year-old from Memphis, Tennessee, said he started listening to Webbon a year ago and initially thought he seemed racist. Goforth eventually saw Webbon as focusing more on “heritage and culture," and was drawn in. Micah Murphy, Goforth’s 18-year-old friend, had a similar view. Webbon “is a little bit on the edgier side" on race, Murphy said, but “I haven’t yet heard him say anything that contradicts Scripture.” Christian nationalists are ready for the next phase Webbon said phase one of his plan was achieved in the midterm wipeout for Republicans. Phase two is expanding the political machinery, such as door-knockers, campaign donors and phone banks. Phase three is winning elected office, “ideally the presidency,” Webbon said in an interview, but at least “we need a couple governors or some Senate races.” Then there's phase four, which is “to get the rest of our guys into serious positions of influence.” Webbon knows his politics are unsavory to the broader American public, and so does Fuentes, but both said they are having discussions with people thinking of running for president. They wouldn't name the possible candidates, recognizing that their association could be a liability. But Webbon thinks the limits of what's acceptable will shift. Right now, he said, the goal is to “break containment.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/christian-nationalists-see-republicans-midterm-125456813.html

item.title: ICE officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying fight
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a “distressing” scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight. Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.” During the confrontation, another passenger “hurled hot coffee on the officers,” the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed. Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. “We are concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306,” the airline said. “We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.” It added that the airline is committed to “treating every guest with dignity and respect.” The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns “directly with the appropriate authorities.” The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would “engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.” Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were “deeply un-American” and called for the agency's abolition. “The video is horrific and it is chilling,” Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. “We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform.” Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. “Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos,” she said. President Donald Trump on Saturday acknowledged yet another cyberattack had hit the federal government — but told Fox News he thinks the hack could come with benefits. “Maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise,” he said. Top national security officials, meanwhile, have insisted the outages have been caused in large part by internal updates and patches to cyber vulnerabilities. “My constituents and I, we believe sometimes in coincidences but maybe sometimes not,” Rep. item.title: 'Data Center Alley' pauses votes on new projects as it rethinks its zoning rules
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Virginia's Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world. Nathan Howard/Bloomberg via Getty Images Virginia's Loudoun County paused legislative data center applications for a year. Loudoun officials say the pause will give the county time to review its data center regulations. Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers worldwide. The Virginia county at the heart of America's data center boom has paused applications for a year. Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors voted for a break on data center and electrical substation applications during a meeting earlier this week. Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, which earned it the nickname "Data Center Alley." Google and many other tech companies have facilities there. The board said the pause will end once it decides on amendments to Loudoun County's comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance. The board initiated a review of its data center and electrical substation policies in February 2024. "The Board's reason for considering pausing action on legislative applications is to allow time for the county to complete the ongoing review of current data center policies and regulations," a press release from Loudoun County said. The county said developers can continue to submit applications during the pause, and Loudoun County staff will continue to review them and schedule hearings with the planning commission. However, the board says there will be no public hearings or votes until the review is complete. The decision could affect 33 active applications, according to the county. Many US towns and cities have paused or outright banned large data center projects as residents debate their impact on communities. Supporters say new data center developments will create jobs and boost local economies. Critics are concerned about how they could affect the environment, utility costs, and their quality of life. Despite support from the Trump administration and influential tech leaders, data centers proved deeply unpopular during the US midterm elections earlier this month, playing a major role in ushering in a so-called "blue wave" of Democratic candidates.
